notes: Complete statutory appeal on special educational provision and waking-day curriculum.

enrichment.short_title: SEN statutory appeal dismissed where tribunal did not unlawfully shift waking-day provision to parents
key_facts: A 12-year-old girl with total blindness and severe global developmental delay had a statement of special educational needs; her parents funded weekly boarding at W School after Rochdale LEA refused to pay.
The mother appealed to the Special Educational Needs Tribunal against the 2002 statement, seeking a residential placement and a 24-hour or waking-day curriculum.
Professor Tobin gave expert evidence that I's unique combination of disabilities required continuous one-to-one teaching and reinforcement throughout daily activities.
The LEA proposed B School with day placement plus partnership with parents, therapists and peripatetic services outside school hours.
The Tribunal rejected residential placement but accepted that a waking-day approach could be delivered through day school plus out-of-school support.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 326 of the Education Act 1996 against a Special Educational Needs Tribunal decision, with the LEA as second respondent.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the Tribunal's decision was not shown to have unlawfully imposed special educational provision on the parents.
enrichment.ratio: Where a tribunal approves a day-school package with parental liaison and outside specialist support, it does not necessarily breach the LEA's statutory duty to provide special educational provision merely because learning continues outside school hours; the critical question is whether the decision directly or indirectly requires parents to deliver provision that remains the authority's legal responsibility.
legal_issues: What counts as special educational provision as opposed to non-educational provision
Whether a waking-day or 24-hour curriculum required residential placement at W School
Whether the Tribunal unlawfully placed educational duties on the parents

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment quashing convictions on dangerous condition construction.

enrichment.short_title: Death by dangerous driving convictions quashed where inherent vehicle design was not a s2A current state

statutes_considered.title: Motor Vehicles (Authorisation of Special Types) General Order 1979

key_facts: Mr Marchant, driving a Matbro TR250 with front grab and rear trailer on a rural road, was stationary on the correct side when a motorcyclist collided with a protruding tyne and died.
The vehicle was an authorised agricultural motor vehicle; section 40A did not apply, but the prosecution pursued both dangerous position and dangerous condition routes.
The jury convicted Mr Muntz as procurer, implying conviction on the dangerous condition case.
Expert evidence accepted that the grab was in the manufacturers' recommended travel position and that a guard would not have prevented the collision.
Neither defendant was responsible for the inherent design of the unit, which had been sold by a reputable dealer and inspected annually.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge; sentence appeals were referred to the full court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; convictions quashed because the dangerous condition case should not have been left to the jury.
enrichment.ratio: For section 2A(2) of the Road Traffic Act 1988, the vehicle's current state implies a state different from its original or manufactured state; where an authorised agricultural vehicle is used in its inherent condition without fault by the driver or owner, prosecution on the dangerous condition basis is inappropriate and unfair.
legal_issues: Whether section 44 disapplication of section 40A also exempts prosecutions under sections 1 and 2
Meaning of current state versus condition in section 2A(2)
Whether prosecution on inherent design was fair where the vehicle was Secretary of State authorised

notes: Complete planning judicial review on roof terrace enforcement and fallback position.

enrichment.short_title: Inspector upheld on roof terrace enforcement where long prior use negated facilitation argument
key_facts: Mr Langdon installed timber decking, planters, fencing and related structures on the flat roof of 13 Ryders Terrace in St John's Wood without planning permission.
Westminster issued an enforcement notice in September 2002 requiring removal, citing visual impact in the conservation area and neighbour privacy concerns.
Affidavits showed the roof had been used as sitting-out space since at least 1984, including periods when decking was rotten or removed.
The inspector dismissed the four-year ground (d) appeal but granted deemed planning permission, treating privacy loss as unchanged by the structures.
The council challenged the inspector's fallback reasoning on four grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court challenge under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to an inspector's decision on an enforcement notice appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; the inspector's treatment of the fallback position and past use was lawful and adequately reasoned.
enrichment.ratio: Where long-established lawful incidental use of a dwellinghouse roof as private sitting-out space is evidenced, an inspector may properly conclude that operational development such as decking and fencing would make no material difference to the extent of that use and may assess the development mainly by its visual impact on a conservation area.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector erred in relying on a fallback roof terrace use
Whether a comparative exercise was required between use with and without the enforced structures
Whether the council had a fair opportunity to respond to the fallback point

notes: Complete judicial review on sale of full electoral register to credit reference agencies.

enrichment.short_title: Sale of full electoral register to credit reference agencies upheld against Robertson challenge

statutes_considered.title: Representation of the People (England and Wales) Regulations 2001
Representation of the People (England and Wales) (Amendment) Regulations 2002

key_facts: Following Robertson No 1, amended regulations created full and edited registers and permitted limited sale of the full register to credit reference agencies under regulation 114.
Mr Robertson challenged regulation 114 as inconsistent with Robertson No 1 and as violating Article 3 of the First Protocol.
He did not attend the listed hearing due to funding and health difficulties; the court heard the merits in his absence.
The Secretary of State and Experian argued Robertson No 1 concerned direct marketing only and that regulation 114 pursued a legitimate aim with minimal interference with voting rights.
Consultation after Robertson No 1 identified fraud prevention, credit access and financial exclusion as public interest justifications.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review heard in absentia after repeated adjournment applications; heard consecutively with the related I-CD challenge.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; regulation 114 was not precluded by Robertson No 1 and was a proportionate interference with the right to vote.
enrichment.ratio: Robertson No 1 held unlawful the sale of the register for direct marketing without opt-out, not all commercial sales; permitting sale of public register data to registered credit reference agencies for defined vetting and anti-fraud purposes falls within the state's wide margin of appreciation under Article 3 of the First Protocol.
legal_issues: Scope of Robertson No 1 on commercial sales of the electoral register
Whether regulation 114 infringes Article 3 of the First Protocol
Whether the court should decide the case in the claimant's absence

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on judicial review and HRA public authority status of HFML.

enrichment.short_title: Private farmers market company held amenable to judicial review after taking over council markets
key_facts: Hampshire County Council established farmers markets under section 33 and later transferred operation to Hampshire Farmers Markets Ltd, a company limited by guarantee.

HFML refused Mr Beer's application to participate in the 2002 programme; Field J quashed the decision for breach of natural justice and held HFML amenable to judicial review and a functional public authority.
Markets were held on publicly owned town-centre sites to which the public had access.
HCC created HFML, seconded staff, provided office support and transferred goodwill without charge.
HCC appealed; HFML did not.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal by Hampshire County Council against a High Court decision quashing HFML's exclusion decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; HFML's decision was amenable to judicial review and made by a hybrid public authority under section 6 HRA.
enrichment.ratio: A private not-for-profit company that steps into a local authority's shoes running public-access markets on public land, created and supported by the authority to perform an economic development function, exercises a sufficient public element for its licensing decisions to be judicially reviewable and to constitute the exercise of a public function under section 6(3)(b) HRA.
legal_issues: Whether HFML's exclusion decision was amenable to judicial review
Whether HFML was a functional public authority under section 6 HRA
Relevance of market cases and the authority's relationship with HFML

notes: Complete interlocutory libel judgment on late Lucas-Box justification application.

enrichment.short_title: Wall Street Journal permitted limited terrorism-funding justification but trial date vacated
key_facts: Al Rajhi Banking sued over a Wall Street Journal article suggesting possible links between the bank and terrorist funding through past associations.
The defendant sought repeated late amendments to plead Lucas-Box meanings and justification after an earlier refusal on 12 June 2003.
Eady J held the article was capable only of Chase level-two meaning: reasonable grounds to suspect knowing or negligent involvement, not mere grounds to investigate.
Most proposed particulars, including the Golden Chain list and address-book links, were rejected as failing the conduct rule or lacking objective grounds.
Permission was granted to plead justification based on banking services to named charities/front organisations and SAAR Foundation links.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application for permission to amend defences and plead justification shortly before trial in libel proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Partial permission granted for sections (7) and (8) particulars only; trial date of 21 July vacated.
enrichment.ratio: In grave libel allegations, Lucas-Box meanings must match the article's natural meaning and pleaded particulars must show objectively reasonable grounds to suspect reprehensible conduct by the claimant; guilt by association, unparticularised FBI material and level-three Chase meanings will not suffice.
legal_issues: Whether late Lucas-Box meanings were permissible
Applicable Chase level of gravity for terrorism funding allegations
Whether proposed particulars satisfied the conduct rule and Evans v Granada standard

enrichment.short_title: IAT must give reasons for refusing extension of time to apply for leave to appeal
key_facts: Mr Tofik, an Iraqi Kurd, lost an asylum appeal before an adjudicator on 24 January 2002.
Solicitors lodged grounds to the Immigration Appeal Tribunal on 8 March 2002, one month late, citing office oversight and correspondence delay.
The IAT responded on 25 April 2002 with only the words Out of time, without addressing rule 18(3).
Collins J and Davis J refused permission for judicial review at first instance.
The Court of Appeal treated the permission application as proceeding in the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal judicial review of the IAT's refusal to extend time for applying for leave to appeal from an immigration adjudicator.
enrichment.outcome: IAT decision quashed; application remitted to another IAT member; Secretary of State ordered to pay costs.
enrichment.ratio: An application for leave to appeal out of time includes any ancillary application to extend time under rule 18(3), and the IAT must give concise reasons for refusing enlargement; a bare Out of time response is legally inadequate where grounds for extension have been advanced.
legal_issues: Whether rule 18(10) requires reasons for refusing time enlargement
Whether a common law duty to give reasons also applies
Whether the solicitors' explanation amounted to special circumstances

enrichment.short_title: I-CD challenge to credit-agency-only electoral register sales failed for lack of consultation and irrationality

statutes_considered.title: Representation of the People (England and Wales) Regulations 2001
Representation of the People (England and Wales) (Amendment) Regulations 2002

key_facts: I-CD Publishing Ltd operated 192.com, a low-cost identity verification service based on the full electoral register.
After Robertson No 1 and the 2002 amendments, regulation 114 permitted sale of the full register only to credit reference agencies carrying on credit reference services.
I-CD challenged regulation 114 as insufficiently consulted, irrational and creating an exclusionary monopoly for Experian, Equifax and Call Credit.
The company failed to engage with post-Robertson consultation and issued proceedings in October 2002.
I-CD also sought declaratory relief that its proposed revised business model would qualify under regulation 114.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review heard with Robertson No 2; I-CD challenged regulation 114 as too restrictive compared with Robertson's too-permissive challenge.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed on all grounds; declaratory relief as to future non-criminality refused.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 114 lawfully limits full-register sales to registered credit reference agencies actually carrying on credit reference services at the time of purchase; the post-Robertson consultation was not unlawfully confined and the regulation is not irrational merely because only established agencies currently qualify.
legal_issues: Whether I-CD was unlawfully excluded from consultation
Whether regulation 114 irrationally created a monopoly
Whether declaratory relief as to future lawful conduct was available

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on partnership liability for solicitor's fraudulent investment scheme.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitors' firm not liable for partner's involvement in preposterous fraudulent investment scheme
key_facts: Mr Ruparelia, a partner in Ruparelia Thaker, participated in a presentation of a purported investment offering a 6000% annualised return secured by escrow.
J.J. Coughlan Ltd transferred USD 500,000 to the firm's client account and lost the money in a fraud involving Mr Hinojosa and GHFC.
Mr Ruparelia made reassuring statements at a meeting on 28 June 1999 and the firm became escrow agent under sham-style agreements.
Mackay J found Mr Ruparelia liable in deceit and for breach of the Escrow Agreement but held the firm not bound because the acts were outside ordinary course of business.
The claimant knew the proposed return was incredible and the agreements contained false recitals.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against High Court dismissal of claims against the solicitor partnership.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the firm was not liable under sections 5 or 10 of the Partnership Act 1890.
enrichment.ratio: A solicitor partner's acts in promoting and documenting an objectively preposterous investment fraud are not of a kind carried on in the ordinary course of a solicitor's business, even if they resemble negotiation and escrow work; sections 5 and 10 require examination of the substance and nature of the transaction, not merely its general classification.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Ruparelia acted in the ordinary course of the firm's business under section 10
Whether the Escrow Agreement bound the firm under section 5
Interaction of ostensible authority and Dubai Aluminium close-connection test

enrichment.short_title: Coroner erred in failing to summon jury for reportable refuse-truck workplace road death

statutes_considered.title: Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 1995
Health and Safety at Work etc Act 1974

key_facts: Stephane Aineto, intoxicated, was crushed under the rear wheels of a SITA refuse collection truck in a pedestrianised Brighton street in July 2001.
The coroner held an inquest without a jury on 19 December 2001 and recorded death by accident.
The truck driver was moving between refuse bins to assess whether loading was needed when the fatal contact occurred.
The claimant argued the death was reportable to the HSE and required a jury under section 8(3)(c).
The HSE later confirmed the incident was reportable under RIDDOR.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review and related section 13 application; court resolved section 8 jury issue as preliminary point.
enrichment.outcome: Verdict quashed; fresh inquest ordered before a different coroner and jury; claimant awarded JR costs, no order on section 13 costs.
enrichment.ratio: Under regulation 10(2)(b) RIDDOR, work connected with loading or unloading includes driving closely related in time, space and purpose to bin-loading operations; where a coroner has reason to suspect such a reportable workplace road death, section 8(3)(c) of the Coroners Act 1988 requires a jury.
legal_issues: Whether the death was caused by a RIDDOR-reportable accident
Whether regulation 10(2)(b) applies only during actual loading or unloading
Whether a fresh inquest should be ordered despite accidental-death likelihood
